messages.subject: new method for comparing modular signal
messages.subject_clean: new method for comparing modular signal
messages.body_plain:
Fellow morphometricians,

I am pleased to announce that we have a new method, based on multivariate effect sizes, for comparing the strength of modular signal across datasets, and among alternative modular hypotheses for the same dataset. The method is implemented in the latest version of geomorph, and description of the approach may be found in Evolution:

https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/evo.13867

Best,

Dean and the geomorph team

--

Dean Adams

messages.subject: Error digitizing landmarks using digitsurface
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I've been trying to digitise some fixed landmarks with digitsurface() on a humerus' ply.

When I finish selecting all of my landmarks, I get the following error:

Error in file(file, "rt") : cannot open the connection
In addition: Warning message:
In file(file, "rt") :
  cannot open file 'template.txt': No such file or directory

I went back and tried again with the example scallop ply, and I got the exact same error:

Error in file(file, "rt") : cannot open the connection
In addition: Warning message:
In file(file, "rt") :
  cannot open file 'template.txt': No such file or directory

I checked and I have the latest Geomorph, rgl, and RRPP versions, so I don't really know how to move forward.

This is the code I used:
library(geomorph)
data("scallopPLY")
my.ply <- scallopPLY$ply
fixed.lms1 <- digitsurface(spec = my.ply, fixed = 4)

Thanks in advanced.

Cheers,
Camilo

messages.subject: Bilat.symmetry function, version upgrade issue?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I was interested in using the compare.CR function, so I decided to take the plunge and upgrade from geomorph 3.0.7 to version 3.1.3.

However, I now run into a problem when re-running the code for bilat.symmetry:

primates_sym <- bilat.symmetry(primates$coords, ind=dimnames(primates$coords)[[3]], side = NULL, replicate=NULL, object.sym=T, land.pairs=pairedLM).

it now gives me the following error:
"Error in matrix(PSh$ANOVA$df[nrow(RSS) + 1], nrow(RSS), ncol(RSS)) :
  non-numeric matrix extent"

Yet, as far as I can see, this is the same data input as before me upgrading (no issues under 3.0.7) and cannot figure out what may be causing the non-numeric matrix extent. I checked to see if perhaps changes were made to this function, but this does not appear to be the case. In order to make sure I didn't do something stupid, I also checked using a published piece of code (not mine) and it now returns to same error (before the upgrade it did not).

Has anybody else encountered this issue, and if so how did you resolve it?

Best wishes,
Katrien

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Bilat.symmetry function, version upgrade issue?
messages.body_plain:
Just a quick note to everyone in the geomorphoverse…

Katrien’s issue was solved by updating RRPP, the main package on which geomorph depends, and which does the “under the hood” workhorse stuff that makes many of the geomorph functions possible.  When installing or updating geomorph, it is a good practice to not trust CRAN (and cannot trust Github in this way at all) that RRPP will also be updated.  Rather, I recommend that when you install or update geomorph, you do the same with RRPP, just to be safe.

We usually submit updates to CRAN for both packages at the same time, so it is possible to get out of sync updating just one.

Happy computing!
Mike

messages.subject: question on how to do regression scores for shape and size
messages.subject_clean: question on how to do regression scores for shape and size
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am a frequent user of geomorph package and when exploring allometry, I usually visualize how shape and size are correlated with the RegScore or CAC plot obtained from procD.allometry. Of course, I also perform procD.lm or procD.pgls to test the significance of the relationship or to obtain the residuals. However, as this function as been reomved in the new version of geomorph, I wonder if it is possible to visualize this kind of plot in an relatively easy way or if there is some reason why they are not longer recommended.

Thank you very much in advance,

Best,

Alberto Martin-Serra

messages.subject: Using group morphol.disparity values in subsequent PGLS anaylsis
messages.subject_clean: Using group morphol.disparity values in subsequent PGLS anaylsis
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm using morphol.disparity to obtain species disparities using a dataset of Proscrustes aligned landmarks for many specimens per species (morphol.disparity(coords~1, groups~species)). I'm avoiding using Foote's partial disparity because my sampling is much uneaven among species.

I was planing to use the value of disparity obtained for each species as a response variable in subsequent PGLS analysis, using other data as covariates/factors (body size, diet, etc). The ideia is to construct alternative models and to test them with AIC, for example.

I was wondering if, since species' morphological disparities are obtained as residuals in this case, this would lead to the undesired biases of using residuals as variables in PGLS (Freckleton 2009)?

Best regards
Daniel Casali

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dean,

Thanks for answering.

Freckleton 2009 mentions the following:

"One of the most common problems in comparative analyses is the use of residuals as data. This arises particularly when researchers wish to control for one variable, particularly body mass, whilst analysing the relationship between other variables. The approach commonly used is to regress the trait of interest on body mass, take the residuals from this regression and use these as data in the subsequent analysis. Despite warnings from the literature (e.g. Garcia‐Berthou, 2001 <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1420-9101.2009.01757.x#b17>; Freckleton, 2002 <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1420-9101.2009.01757.x#b11>), this approach nevertheless continues to be used in numerous studies.

The problem with doing this is that if the variable controlled for covaries with other variables in the analysis, then subsequent analyses will be biased (Freckleton, 2002 <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1420-9101.2009.01757.x#b11>). The obvious, and straightforward, way to deal with this is to use a multiple regression/linear model in which the confounding variable is used to control for unwanted effects. Subsequently, if required, alternative decomposition of variance can be used to eliminate variables in different orders. For example, if we have two predictors, then the model sequential sums of squares can be examined to see whether the variance explained by predictor 1 is dependent or not of predictor 2 in the model, and to decide whether the ordering of the variables is important. Detailed examples of this process, and consequences for interpretation, are given by Grafen & Hails (2004) <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1420-9101.2009.01757.x#b22>."

In the case of disparities obtained with geomorph, I was initially thinking to regress my shape data on cs_size, but, as far as I understood, this could fall into the problem mentioned in Freckleton 2009. In the case of just obtaining disparities per species and leave the inclusion of cs_size for subsequent PGLS analysis, I'm just summarizing disparity per groups, and this problem may not apply, is this it?

Best

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Agh; that is helpful.  This is a general problem, but not for the case of disparity you mentioned. What Freckleton is (correctly) worried about is eliminating covariation in one variable so one can analyze the pattern one ‘wanted’ to analyze. An example:

A researcher wishes to look at shape across species, however shape varies with size. So the researcher decides to first do a regression of shape ~ size (ie allometry), and remove the effect of size by using residuals in: shape.residual ~ group.

This one should not do, and is what Freckleton is talking about.  This ‘logical’ stepwise implementation has been around for decades, and is not the way to go. Instead, run the full factorial model: shape ~ size + group + size:gp.  This is an ancova; or for 2 continuous variables a multiple regression.  The issue with residuals from one analysis used as data for another is that it ignores covariation of model effects, embodied by their interaction.  For my group and size example, if the allometry differs among groups, then using size-adjusted residuals has now conflated group differences with allometric differences. That is hard to sort out.  Using the full factorial model properly accounts for things.

Regardless, that is not how the residuals stated in the disparity analysis are using things, so this concern at least is alleviated.

Dean

Freckleton 2009 mentions the following:

"One of the most common problems in comparative analyses is the use of residuals as data. This arises particularly when researchers wish to control for one variable, particularly body mass, whilst analysing the relationship between other variables. The approach commonly used is to regress the trait of interest on body mass, take the residuals from this regression and use these as data in the subsequent analysis. Despite warnings from the literature (e.g. Garcia‐Berthou, 2001 <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1420-9101.2009.01757.x#b17>; Freckleton, 2002 <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1420-9101.2009.01757.x#b11>), this approach nevertheless continues to be used in numerous studies.

The problem with doing this is that if the variable controlled for covaries with other variables in the analysis, then subsequent analyses will be biased (Freckleton, 2002 <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1420-9101.2009.01757.x#b11>). The obvious, and straightforward, way to deal with this is to use a multiple regression/linear model in which the confounding variable is used to control for unwanted effects. Subsequently, if required, alternative decomposition of variance can be used to eliminate variables in different orders. For example, if we have two predictors, then the model sequential sums of squares can be examined to see whether the variance explained by predictor 1 is dependent or not of predictor 2 in the model, and to decide whether the ordering of the variables is important. Detailed examples of this process, and consequences for interpretation, are given by Grafen & Hails (2004) <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1420-9101.2009.01757.x#b22>."

In the case of disparities obtained with geomorph, I was initially thinking to regress my shape data on cs_size, but, as far as I understood, this could fall into the problem mentioned in Freckleton 2009. In the case of just obtaining disparities per species and leave the inclusion of cs_size for subsequent PGLS analysis, I'm just summarizing disparity per groups, and this problem may not apply, is this it?

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Geomorph, Stereomorph and CVA
messages.body_plain:
Mateus,

after performing a gpa of your data to extract shape variables, you can do a CVA with the general functions available for that (e.g. function lda in package MASS), after somehow removing the redundant dimensions in your data that result from the gpa. However, as GM data are particular, I would recommend you rather look at bayesian classification methods, i.e. available through the function classify in the package RRPP.

Hope this helps

Antigoni
